events.text: The temple of the god stands at the top of a hundred worn steps at the end of your street, and the steps are the first mountain of your life. Every morning the grown-ups climb them to pray. This morning, while nobody is looking, you start climbing too, on your hands and knees.

choices.text: Climb all the way to the top

effects.log: You climb a hundred steps and arrive at the top filthy, triumphant and badly out of breath, at the feet of a stone statue of the god. An old priest finds you there and laughs until the incense shakes.

choices.text: Stop halfway and look at the town

effects.log: Halfway up you sit and look back. The whole town is below you, roofs and smoke and washing. It is the first time you understand that the world is large. You sit there until somebody fetches you.

choices.text: Pick the little flowers growing in the cracks

effects.log: You come back down with a fist of crushed yellow flowers and give them to the first person you meet, who happens to be the baker. The baker gives you a bun. A lifelong friendship begins.

events.text: There is a cat who lives on the temple steps, a fat grey one the priests call the God's Doorkeeper, and it decides who may come up. It looks at you the way a judge looks at a thief.

choices.text: Offer it the crust of your bun

effects.log: The Doorkeeper eats the crust with great dignity and lets you pass. From then on it walks up the steps beside you, every morning, like an escort.

choices.text: Sit down and wait for it to decide

effects.log: You sit. The cat sits. You wait the whole morning. In the end the cat yawns and moves aside, and an old priest says that is more patience than most grown-ups have.

choices.text: Step over it

effects.log: You step over it. It bites your ankle, not hard, and you cry, and everyone agrees the Doorkeeper was right.

events.text: The priests find you one morning sitting in the lap of the god's statue, which nobody is allowed to touch, looking perfectly at home. There is a gasp. The oldest priest comes running with her robe held up in both hands.

choices.text: Say it is a comfortable lap

effects.log: The old priest stares at you, and then, to everyone's horror, laughs. 'It was made for it,' she says. 'Get down, little one, before the others faint.' After that she slips you a honey-cake every week.

choices.text: Climb down and apologise to the statue

effects.log: You climb down and bow to the statue, which you feel owes you nothing. The priests are so moved they let you ring the morning bell.

choices.text: Ask why the god looks so sad up close

effects.log: The oldest priest looks at the stone face for a long time. 'Nobody has ever asked me that,' she says. She does not answer. You think she does not know either.

events.text: Every child of {pw_world} learns the Little Questions at the temple school, sitting cross-legged on reed mats while a young priest asks and the whole room answers. Who made the world? The god made the world. How did the god deal with us? The god {pw_record}. What does the god want? Here the room always goes quiet, because nobody knows.

choices.text: Learn every answer by heart

effects.log: You learn all the answers in a week and can say them faster than the priest. The priest is proud and slightly alarmed.

choices.text: Shout an answer to the last question

effects.log: 'Breakfast,' you shout. The room explodes. The priest keeps a straight face for nearly a breath, then gives up.

choices.text: Ask why the god does not just tell us

effects.log: The priest says the god is busy. You think of all the things you are busy with and decide the god must have a great many chores.

events.text: Recitation Day: the children of the temple school stand up one by one before the whole town and say the Little Questions without a mistake. Grandparents cry. One small child always forgets everything and is cheered anyway.

choices.text: Recite perfectly

effects.log: You recite without a single slip, and the old people nod at each other as if they made you themselves. Someone gives you a paper star.

choices.text: Help the child who forgets

effects.log: You stand beside the forgetful child and whisper every answer. You both finish together. The cheering is louder than for anyone.

choices.text: Add an answer of your own

effects.log: When the priest asks what the god wants, you say: to see what we do next. The square goes quiet in a different way. Later three old people come to shake your hand.

events.text: The young priest of the temple school asks you to stay behind. 'You asked a question years ago,' the priest says, 'about why the god does not tell us. I have been thinking about it ever since. What do you think now?'

choices.text: Say the god is waiting to be asked properly

effects.log: The priest writes that down, in the margin of the temple book, next to the Little Questions. It is still there, in your handwriting, when you are old.

choices.text: Say the god made us to work it out

effects.log: The priest smiles slowly. 'That is what I was afraid of,' the priest says, and gives you the key to the school library.

choices.text: Say you think the god is lonely

effects.log: The priest is quiet for a long while, and then puts a hand on your head, which has never happened before, and sends you home with an apple.

events.text: In {pw_world} every cradle has the same song, and your mother, {npc}, sings it to you every night: Hush now, the Maker made the stars, the Maker made the sea, the Maker {pw_record} and the Maker watches thee. You do not know the words yet. You know the tune better than your own name.

choices.text: Fall asleep to it

effects.log: You sleep every night by the second line. Your mother says you are the easiest child in the street, and the street agrees.

choices.text: Hum along, out of tune

effects.log: You hum, terribly, and your mother laughs so much {he} cannot finish the song. It becomes a game: you hum, {he} laughs, and nobody sleeps.

choices.text: Reach for the stars through the window

effects.log: You reach for the stars every night while {he} sings, as if you could pull one down. Your father says you will be a stargazer. Your mother says you will be trouble.

events.text: You have made up a new verse to the Maker's Lullaby, and it is about the Maker being tired and wanting a snack. Your parents are trying very hard not to laugh in front of your grandmother, who is devout.

choices.text: Sing it to your grandmother

effects.log: Your grandmother listens to the end, stern as a stone. Then, at last: 'Well, the Maker probably was.' The verse is sung in your house forever after.

choices.text: Sing it only to the cat

effects.log: The cat approves. It is the only one in the house who hears the snack verse, and it keeps the secret.

choices.text: Make up a sadder verse instead

effects.log: Your new verse is about the Maker being alone in the dark before the world. Your mother, {npc}, stops sewing. {He} asks you, gently, where you heard that. You did not hear it anywhere.

events.text: A new baby has come to the house next door, and it will not stop crying. Its parents are grey with tiredness. They knock on your door at midnight, ashamed, asking if anyone knows a trick. Your mother, {npc}, looks at you.

choices.text: Sing it the Maker's Lullaby

effects.log: You sing the old song at the baby's cradle, quietly, all the verses. The baby stares at you and falls asleep mid-howl. The neighbours look at you as if you were a small miracle.

choices.text: Sing it the snack verse

effects.log: The baby stops crying to listen, then laughs, then sleeps. Its parents ask for the words. In ten years every child in the street knows the snack verse.

choices.text: Fetch your mother

effects.log: Your mother walks the baby up and down the yard for an hour and it sleeps. You learn that grown-ups also do not know the trick; they only keep walking.

events.text: At supper, quite calmly, you mention that you made the sky. Not all of it, you add, to be fair: the stars took a long time and you did the moon in a hurry. The table goes silent. A spoon is put down.

choices.text: Explain how you did the moon

effects.log: You explain, with gestures, that the moon is a little lopsided because you were tired. Nobody can prove you wrong. An older cousin goes outside to look and comes back pale.

choices.text: Say it was a dream

effects.log: You say it was a dream, because their faces frighten you. The grown-ups laugh with relief. You know it was not a dream. You keep it, like a stone in a pocket.

choices.text: Point to the star you are proudest of

effects.log: You take everyone outside and point to a small blue star low in the east. It flickers, very slightly, as if it heard you. Nobody sleeps much that night.

events.text: The story has got about: there is a child in the village who says they made the world. The children call you Little Maker, sometimes kindly. A priest comes from the next town to test you with questions about the beginning.

choices.text: Answer the priest truthfully

effects.log: You answer from memory: the first light was colder than anyone thinks, and the first sound was a laugh, not a word. The priest writes it all down with a shaking hand and leaves without saying goodbye.

choices.text: Pretend to be an ordinary child

effects.log: You get every question wrong on purpose. The priest goes away disappointed and the village forgets. Only you remember, and the remembering gets quieter.

choices.text: Ask the priest a question back

effects.log: You ask the priest what the god should have done differently. The priest has come to test you and goes home tested. Later you hear the priest preached on it for a month.

events.text: The memories are fading as you grow, the way dreams fade at breakfast. Some nights you can still see the world from above, small and bright and turning. Some nights you cannot. Your oldest friend asks you, seriously, whether you still remember being a god.

choices.text: Say yes, and that it does not matter

effects.log: 'I remember,' you say. 'But I would rather be here.' Your friend thinks about this and then nods, and you go and throw stones in the river, which no god ever had time to do.

choices.text: Write the memories down before they go

effects.log: You fill a notebook with everything: the cold first light, the lopsided moon, the laugh. You hide it under a floorboard. Some day somebody will find it and argue about it for a century.

choices.text: Say no, and let them go

effects.log: 'No,' you say, and as you say it, it becomes a little more true. You feel lighter, and a little sad, as if you had waved off a ship.

events.text: Pilgrims pass through your village every spring on the long road to the great temple of the god, and this year one family stops to mend a cart wheel. Their child, {npc}, has walked four hundred miles and has opinions about every one of them.

choices.text: Show {npc} the best climbing tree

mem.note: was my friend when my family walked the pilgrim road

effects.log: You and {npc} spend the whole day in the tree, trading stories. {npc} has seen the sea. You have seen a two-headed calf. It is a fair trade.

choices.text: Trade your carved whistle for a pilgrim's shell

mem.note: was my friend when my family walked the pilgrim road

effects.log: {npc} gives you a shell from the far coast, pierced for a string. You give {npc} your best whistle. You both feel you have the better of it.

choices.text: Ask why they are walking so far

mem.note: was my friend when my family walked the pilgrim road

effects.log: {npc} says the family is walking to thank the god for a good harvest, and also because walking is the only time anyone in the family stops arguing. You understand this completely.

events.text: {npc} comes back up the road a year later on the way home, browner, taller, and full of the great temple: a roof of gold, a bell the size of a house, ten thousand candles, and in the middle, a statue of the god that {npc} insists looks a bit like you.

choices.text: Laugh it off

mem.note: was my friend when my family walked the pilgrim road

effects.log: You laugh. {npc} does not. {npc} keeps looking at you sideways for the whole visit, and leaves you a candle stub from the great temple, still smelling of a thousand prayers.

choices.text: Ask exactly what the statue's face was like

mem.note: was my friend when my family walked the pilgrim road

effects.log: {npc} describes it carefully: tired eyes, a mouth that seems about to say something. You go home and look in the water trough for a long time.

choices.text: Wear the shell where {npc} can see it

mem.note: was my friend when my family walked the pilgrim road

effects.log: {npc} sees the shell on its string round your neck and goes red with pleasure, then pulls out your old whistle, worn smooth from a year of being played.

events.text: A letter comes, in a pilgrim's careful hand, carried by a trader: {npc}'s family is coming back to settle in your valley, because, {npc} writes, there is a tree there that is worth walking four hundred miles for.

choices.text: Run to the tree and wait for them

mem.note: was my friend when my family walked the pilgrim road

effects.log: You wait in the tree for three days. On the third, a cart comes round the bend, and {npc} is standing up in it, waving with both arms. Your valley has a new family, and you have a friend for life.

choices.text: Help get a house ready for them

mem.note: was my friend when my family walked the pilgrim road

effects.log: You and the neighbours patch up the empty cottage by the mill. When {npc}'s family arrives there is soup on the fire. {npc}'s parent weeps, which makes your neighbours weep too.

choices.text: Write back that you will show them everything

mem.note: was my friend when my family walked the pilgrim road

effects.log: You write a long letter listing everything worth seeing: the tree, the calf, the place the river goes underground. {npc} arrives with your letter folded small and worn soft from reading.

events.text: Once a year, on the Night of Small Lanterns, the children of {pw_world} make paper lanterns, one each, and set them on the water for the god to see. Each lantern is shaped like something the god did, as the priests tell it, so the river fills with tiny paper suns and seas and open hands.

choices.text: Make a lantern shaped like the sun

effects.log: Your sun is lopsided and burns very bright, and it floats further than anyone else's. The old people say a far-floating lantern means a long life.

choices.text: Make a lantern shaped like yourself

effects.log: Your lantern is a little paper you. The other children think it is very rude, or very funny. You think it is only honest.

choices.text: Help a younger child fold one

effects.log: You fold a paper fish for a small child who cannot manage. The child's whole family thanks you, and the fish floats beautifully.

events.text: This year you are old enough to stay up for the end of the Night of Small Lanterns, when the priests read the god's deeds over the water: that the god {pw_record}. Then everyone is silent, and listens, in case the god answers. The god never does.

choices.text: Listen as hard as you can

effects.log: You listen until your ears ring. Just before the end you are sure you hear something, far off, like someone in another room laughing gently. You never tell anyone.

choices.text: Whisper an answer for the god

effects.log: In the silence you whisper, very quietly: I see them. A grandmother beside you jumps and stares at you. She says nothing, but squeezes your hand all the way home.

choices.text: Fall asleep against your neighbour

effects.log: You fall asleep in the silence, which the priests say is the best way to listen. You wake up being carried home, with lantern paper in your hair.

events.text: You are chosen to carry the first lantern this year, the big one, the shape of the whole world of {pw_world}, down to the water at the head of all the children. It is heavier than it looks, and the wind is getting up.

choices.text: Carry it steadily through the wind

ok.log: You carry the world down to the river without a tear in it, and set it on the water, and the little lanterns follow it out like ducklings. People talk about it for a year.

fail.log: A gust takes it and the paper world catches fire halfway down. The crowd groans, then cheers, because a burning world on the water is, they decide, rather beautiful.

choices.text: Ask a friend to carry the other side

effects.log: You carry the world together, one at each edge. The priests say that is the first time the big lantern has gone down with two bearers. They decide they like it.

choices.text: Shelter it inside your coat

effects.log: You walk the world down to the water bent double, wrapped in your coat. It arrives crumpled and alive. Your coat smells of smoke all winter.

events.text: The favourite game of the children of {pw_world} is God and Mortals: one child stands on the well cover and is the god, and the others come one by one to ask for things, and the god must give or refuse, and everyone argues about whether it was fair.

choices.text: Be a mortal and ask for something enormous

effects.log: You ask the god for a mountain made of honey-cake. The god, a solemn child of six, grants it at once. Everyone agrees this is a very good god.

choices.text: Ask the god for nothing, and see what happens

effects.log: You kneel and ask for nothing. The god is confused, then furious, then grants you a stick. You keep the stick for years.

choices.text: Refuse to play, and watch

effects.log: You watch from the wall and notice that the children always want the god to say yes, and then do not trust a god who always says yes.

events.text: Today it is your turn to stand on the well cover and be the god. The other children line up. The first one asks for the rain to stop. The second asks for the rain to keep going, for the frogs.

choices.text: Grant both, by making it rain only on the frogs

effects.log: You declare it will rain only on the frogs. The children argue about it for a whole afternoon and decide it was the wisest thing a god has ever said on that well.

choices.text: Refuse both and tell them to share umbrellas

effects.log: The mortals are outraged. Then, grudgingly, they share umbrellas. It is the most peaceful afternoon in the history of the game.

choices.text: Step down and let the smallest child be god

effects.log: The smallest child stands on the well and grants everything, including a pony, to everyone. It is a very popular reign.

events.text: A grown-up has been watching your games of God and Mortals: the old priest from the temple, leaning on the fence. 'Tell me,' the priest asks you, 'when you are the god, is it hard?'

choices.text: Say it is the hardest game there is

effects.log: 'Everyone wants something different,' you say, 'and they all mean it.' The old priest is quiet for a moment and then laughs, kindly. 'Yes,' the priest says. 'Yes. I always wondered.'

choices.text: Say it is easy if you listen first

effects.log: The old priest raises an eyebrow and asks for lessons. You give them, on the well cover, with great seriousness, and the priest takes notes.

choices.text: Say the real god must be tired

effects.log: The old priest looks at you strangely and says, 'The real one must be very tired indeed.' Then the priest buys every child in the game a sugared plum.

events.text: In {pw_world} the cultivation of the body and spirit is taught in small schools that grew, the priests say, from the god's own teachings, passed down for {pw_years} years and argued over for most of them. The school in your town takes children at seven, in a courtyard with a plum tree, and the first lesson is only this: breathe.

choices.text: Breathe the way the teacher shows

effects.log: You breathe in for four, hold for four, out for four, until the courtyard seems to breathe with you. The teacher, a stout woman with flour on her sleeves, looks at you twice.

choices.text: Breathe your own way

effects.log: You breathe the way that feels right, slower, deeper, with a little pause at the top like a bird turning. The teacher stops the whole class to watch. Nobody knows what to say.

choices.text: Fall asleep in the sun

effects.log: You fall asleep under the plum tree, breathing very evenly. The teacher lets you, saying it is the oldest lesson there is.

events.text: The second year at the breath school: the teacher brings out the founder's scroll, the oldest thing in the town, a page of the god's teaching copied and recopied for {pw_years} years. The children may each look at it once.

choices.text: Read it slowly

effects.log: You read it slowly, and something odd happens: you know what the next line will say before your eyes reach it. The teacher sees your lips moving ahead of the words and goes very pale.

choices.text: Point out a copying mistake

effects.log: There is a mistake in the third line, a word copied wrong a thousand years ago, and you can see it as clearly as a crooked picture. The teacher checks the oldest copy in the temple. You are right.

choices.text: Only look at the drawings in the margin

effects.log: Someone, long ago, drew a little bird in the margin of the scroll. You love the bird. The teacher says the bird is the most argued-about thing in all of cultivation.

events.text: The breath school's yearly test: each child must sit by the pond without moving from sunrise until the plum blossom falls, and then show what they have learned. The parents watch from the wall with picnic baskets.

choices.text: Sit still until the blossom falls

ok.log: You sit through the morning, and somewhere around noon you feel your breath and the pond's surface become one thing. When the blossom falls, it lands in your open hand. The teacher bows to you.

fail.log: A dragonfly lands on your nose and you sneeze, and the whole wall laughs. The teacher says sneezing is also a kind of breath and passes you anyway.

choices.text: Teach the breath to the child beside you

effects.log: The child beside you is panicking. You breathe with them, quietly, four and four and four. You both pass. The teacher says that was the real test.

choices.text: Breathe your own way, the slow way

effects.log: You breathe your own slow way, with the pause at the top. The pond goes still around you, and the fish come to look. The teacher writes your way down for the school.

events.text: On summer nights the meadows of {pw_world} fill with lamp-moths, creatures found nowhere else, each one glowing the colour of what it last ate: blue for flax, gold for clover, red for the wild roses. The priests say the god made them because the first night was too dark.

choices.text: Chase them with a jar

effects.log: You catch a golden one in a jar and carry it home like treasure. It lights your room all night, and in the morning you let it go, as the grown-ups say you must.

choices.text: Lie still and let them land on you

effects.log: You lie in the grass and the moths settle on you one by one until you glow all over, blue and gold and red. The grown-ups find you by your light.

choices.text: Watch from the doorstep

effects.log: You watch from the doorstep with your chin on your knees. The meadow looks like the sky has come down to rest. You fall asleep there, happy.

events.text: You have discovered that you can make a lamp-moth any colour you like by what you feed it, and you have been very busy. There is a purple one in a box under your bed. Nobody has ever seen a purple lamp-moth.

choices.text: Show the purple moth to the temple

effects.log: The priests are thrilled and baffled. The oldest one says the god must be pleased with you, to show you a new colour. You suspect it was the blackberries.

choices.text: Make one for every child in the street

effects.log: By the end of the summer every child in the street has a moth of a different colour. The street glows like a festival every night, and parents complain, delighted.

choices.text: Let the purple one go into the meadow

effects.log: You let it go. Next summer there are a dozen purple moths in the meadow, and the next, a hundred. You made that, you think, and you are not sure how you feel about it.

events.text: A cold summer: the lamp-moths are few and dim, and the old people say a dark summer is bad luck. The children are told to stay in. But you know a meadow over the hill where the wild roses still bloom.

choices.text: Lead the dim moths to the roses

effects.log: You walk the dark meadow with a lantern and a stick of honey, coaxing the dim moths over the hill. By midnight the rose meadow burns red, and the next morning the old people stop talking about bad luck.

choices.text: Plant clover around the village

effects.log: You spend a week planting clover in every gap. It takes two summers, but the gold moths come back to the village and stay.

choices.text: Ask the temple to pray for the moths

effects.log: The priests are touched to be asked. The whole temple prays for the lamp-moths on a Tuesday. Whether it works or not, the town feels better.

events.text: Every household in {pw_world} leaves a small bowl of rice and fruit at the god's niche by the door, and it is the children's job to fill it. Today you and {npc} are fighting over whose turn it is, and the plum in the bowl is looking very fine.

choices.text: Let {npc} fill it

mem.note: filled the offering bowl with me

effects.log: You let {npc} have the turn. {npc} fills the bowl with enormous ceremony, then gives you half of the plum, which is not allowed. You both feel very wicked and very close.

choices.text: Fill it together

mem.note: filled the offering bowl with me

effects.log: You fill it together, arguing about where each grape goes. The result is lopsided. The god, you both agree, will understand.

choices.text: Eat the plum and blame the god

mem.note: filled the offering bowl with me

effects.log: You eat the plum. {npc} tells. Everyone is very cross, and the old priest says the god has seen worse.

events.text: {npc} has fallen ill with a fever, and the grown-ups are worried, and you are sent out of the room. You go and sit by the god's niche, where the offering bowl is empty because nobody remembered today.

choices.text: Fill the bowl with your own supper

mem.note: filled the offering bowl with me

effects.log: You put your whole supper in the bowl and sit beside it all night. In the morning {npc}'s fever has broken. You are very hungry and do not care.

choices.text: Talk to the god about {npc}

mem.note: filled the offering bowl with me

effects.log: You tell the god everything about {npc}: the good, the annoying, the plum. You say you would like to keep {him}, please. {npc} gets better. You decide it was probably the medicine. Probably.

choices.text: Sneak in to sit with {npc}

mem.note: filled the offering bowl with me

effects.log: You sneak in and sit at the end of the bed and tell {npc} stories until you are both asleep. The grown-ups find you and are too tired to be cross.

events.text: You and {npc} are old enough now to take the offering bowl to the town temple on feast day, alone, through the crowds. {npc} wants to go the long way, past the sweet stalls. You want to go the right way.

choices.text: Go the long way with {npc}

mem.note: filled the offering bowl with me

effects.log: You go the long way. You arrive late, sticky and laughing, and the bowl has one fewer plum in it than it should. The priest at the door pretends not to count.

choices.text: Go the right way and buy {npc} a sweet on the way home

mem.note: filled the offering bowl with me

effects.log: You go the right way and arrive first, and on the way home you buy {npc} a sugar bird. {npc} says you are the best and most boring sibling in the world.

choices.text: Let {npc} carry the bowl

mem.note: filled the offering bowl with me

effects.log: {npc} carries the bowl the whole way, with a face like a priest. You walk behind as the procession. It is the proudest you have ever seen {him}.

events.text: In {pw_world} a child is carried to the temple in the first years of life to have their name written in the great book beside the god's deeds. Your parents carry you up the steps in your best clothes, and you are sick on the priest.

choices.text: Cry all the way through

effects.log: You cry through the whole blessing. The priest says loud children have strong lungs and long lives, which is what priests always say, and writes your name in the book.

choices.text: Grab the priest's pen

effects.log: You grab the pen and make a large blot in the book next to your name. The priest says it is a sign. Your parents agree, because they are proud of you and the blot.

choices.text: Laugh at the candles

effects.log: You laugh at the candles all through the ceremony, and the priest laughs too, and loses the place, and has to start the blessing again.

events.text: You ask your parents why they chose your name. They look at each other, and say it is from the priests' reading: a word from the oldest part of the book, the part that tells how the god {pw_record}.

choices.text: Ask what it means

effects.log: It means something like the one who comes back, they tell you. You think about that for a long time, on the roof, where you are not allowed.

choices.text: Say you would rather be called something else

effects.log: You announce you would like to be called Badger. For a month your whole family calls you Badger, very seriously. Then you change your mind, and they are relieved.

choices.text: Say it fits

effects.log: You say it fits you. Your parents laugh, but one of them looks at you a little longer than usual.

events.text: The temple lets the children look at the great book on their naming day each year, and this year you find your own name for the first time, small and careful in the priest's hand, a few pages after the god's last deed.

choices.text: Trace your name with a finger

effects.log: You trace the letters of your name, then turn back the pages to the god's deeds. The handwriting there is older, but somehow, oddly, it feels like your own.

choices.text: Find the blot

effects.log: There is the blot, a huge black splash beside your name, and in the margin someone has drawn it a little face. You laugh so loudly the priests come running.

choices.text: Count how many names come between you and the god

effects.log: You count the names, page by page, all afternoon. There are more than you can count. You feel very small and part of something very large.

events.text: Beyond the orchards there is an old temple of the god that nobody uses, roofless, full of birds, with a statue whose face has been worn smooth by rain. The grown-ups say it is unsafe. The children say it is the best place in {pw_world}.

choices.text: Explore it with a friend

effects.log: You and a friend explore every corner and find a carved stone with the god's hand on it and a nest of baby owls. You promise to keep the owls a secret forever.

choices.text: Clean the statue's face

effects.log: You scrub the moss from the statue's face with a rag and a bucket. Under it, faintly, the carved face is smiling. You did not expect that.

choices.text: Stay away as you are told

effects.log: You stay away. You hear about the owls from other children and are envious for a week. The grown-ups are very pleased with you.

events.text: You find a box under a loose stone in the old temple: a wooden box, dry inside, holding a child's carving of the god, rough and lovingly made, and a note so old the ink is brown. It says: For the god, from someone small.

choices.text: Put it on the altar where it belongs

effects.log: You set the little carving on the broken altar. It looks right there, as if it had been waiting. The birds watch you do it.

choices.text: Take it to the town priest

effects.log: The priest holds the carving in both hands and goes quiet. 'This is older than the town,' the priest says. It is put in the new temple, with your name on a card beneath it.

choices.text: Add a carving of your own

effects.log: You whittle a little figure of your own, badly, and put it beside the old one, with a note: For the god, from someone else small. You feel you have answered a letter.

events.text: The town council has decided to pull down the old temple for its stones. The children are horrified. A meeting is called in the square, and for the first time, a child stands up to speak at it: you.

choices.text: Speak for the old temple

ok.log: You speak about the owls and the smiling face and the little carving. The square is quiet. The council votes to leave the old temple standing, and the owls stay.

fail.log: Your voice shakes and you forget half of it. The council takes the stones anyway, but leaves the statue and the altar standing in the orchard, which you decide is a victory.

choices.text: Organise the children to repair it instead

effects.log: Forty children carry stones up the orchard path for a month and patch the walls. The council, embarrassed, sends a builder. The old temple gets a roof.

choices.text: Ask the owls' permission first

effects.log: You climb up to the owls and ask them, solemnly, what they want. They look at you. You report back that the owls say no. Somehow, it works.

events.text: A new baby has come to your house, red-faced and loud, and everyone is very busy with it. Your grandmother says that in {pw_world} the god gives every new baby a gift, and it is the older child's job to find out what it is.

choices.text: Watch the baby very carefully

effects.log: You watch the baby for a week and decide its gift is shouting. Your grandmother says that is a gift too, in its way.

choices.text: Give the baby your favourite toy

effects.log: You put your wooden horse in the cradle. The baby grabs it and will not let go. Your parents look at you as if you had done something very grown-up.

choices.text: Ask the god what the gift is

effects.log: You ask the god at the niche by the door. You do not get an answer, but the baby stops crying for the first time in three days, which seems like one.

events.text: The baby has started to walk, and walks only towards you, like a moth to a lantern. Your parents call you the baby's god, because it follows you everywhere and believes everything you say.

choices.text: Teach it the Little Questions

effects.log: You teach the baby to say: who made the world? You! It shouts this at visitors. The priest who comes to tea does not know where to look.

choices.text: Teach it to walk properly

effects.log: You walk up and down the yard with the baby holding your fingers until it can walk alone. Then it runs away from you at once, and you are proud and a bit offended.

choices.text: Hide from it

effects.log: You hide, and the baby cries, and you come out, and it laughs. You learn that being followed is a responsibility.

events.text: The little one is old enough for the temple school now, and on the first day, at the door, will not let go of your sleeve. The other children are watching.

choices.text: Walk in together

effects.log: You walk in together, holding hands, in front of everyone, and sit together the whole morning. Nobody laughs. Some of them wish they had an older sibling like you.

choices.text: Tell the little one the god is watching, and is proud

effects.log: You say the god is watching and is very proud. The little one lets go of your sleeve and marches in. You are not sure where the words came from.

choices.text: Say: who made the world?

effects.log: The little one shouts: you did! The whole school turns to stare at you. The teacher laughs so hard the lesson starts late. The little one goes in happily, sure of the world.

events.text: The children of your town keep a weather-stick by the temple door, a peeled willow wand with notches, and every morning one of them must guess what weather the god will send, and cut a notch for right or wrong. Nobody has ever been right seven days running.

choices.text: Guess from the clouds

effects.log: You lie on your back and read the clouds like a book. You are right four days in a row, then wrong spectacularly. The stick records both.

choices.text: Guess from the old cat's mood

effects.log: You guess by whether the temple cat is grumpy. You are right three days running. The children consider electing the cat.

choices.text: Always guess sunshine

effects.log: You guess sunshine every day, because you want it. You are right twice. The other children say that is not a method, that is a wish. You say the god likes wishes.

events.text: You are on six days right in a row. The whole town knows. On the seventh morning there is a crowd at the temple door, and the sky is doing absolutely nothing in either direction.

choices.text: Guess rain

effects.log: You say rain. There is a long, tense pause, and then one fat drop falls on the priest's head. The crowd roars. You are carried around the square on shoulders, in the drizzle.

choices.text: Say you do not know

effects.log: You say, honestly, that today you do not know. The crowd is disappointed, then thoughtful. The priest says it was the wisest guess on the stick.

choices.text: Ask the god out loud for a sign

effects.log: You ask the sky, politely, for a hint. A single rainbow appears, with no rain at all. Nobody knows how to notch that.

events.text: Your weather-stick is so famous that a farmer from the far valley comes to ask whether to plant this week or next. A whole year's food might hang on what you say.

choices.text: Tell the truth: it is only a game

effects.log: You tell the farmer it is a children's game and a lucky stick. The farmer thanks you for your honesty, plants anyway, and sends you a sack of apples in autumn.

choices.text: Read the sky as carefully as you can

effects.log: You spend a whole day watching the sky and the birds, and say: next week. It rains hard the week after that. The far valley has a good harvest.

choices.text: Take the farmer to the oldest farmer in town

effects.log: You take the farmer to old Hesk, who has watched the weather for seventy years. They talk for an afternoon. You learn more listening than in a year of guessing.

events.text: On your island the children learn to swim with the sea-calves, round grey creatures the size of a pig, with whiskers and sad eyes, that the priests say the god made to keep children from drowning. A sea-calf will not let a child sink. Everyone knows it. Nobody knows why.

choices.text: Paddle out to the sea-calves

effects.log: A sea-calf comes and lies under you in the water like a raft, and breathes, and you float on its breathing. You learn to swim that summer without ever being afraid.

choices.text: Feed them fish heads from the beach

effects.log: The sea-calves come to the edge of the water and take the fish heads from your hand with great politeness. One of them follows you along the beach.

choices.text: Stay in the shallows and watch

effects.log: You watch the sea-calves from the shallows, chin in the water. They watch you back. It seems to you that both sides are learning something.

events.text: One sea-calf has taken to you, a small one with a white patch over one eye. It waits for you at the jetty every morning, and sulks when you go to the temple school instead.

choices.text: Name it after the god

effects.log: You call it Maker. The priests are scandalised and then, privately, charmed. The whole island calls it Maker within a week.

choices.text: Teach it to fetch shells

effects.log: You teach it to fetch shells, and it teaches you to hold your breath for a very long time, which seems a fair exchange.

choices.text: Take it to the temple school

effects.log: You bring it to the steps of the temple school, where it lies in the sun and listens to the lessons. The teacher gives up and lets it stay.

events.text: A storm has come up quickly, and a boat with three small children in it has broken loose from the jetty and is drifting towards the reef. The grown-ups are out fishing. The sea-calves are barking on the rocks.

choices.text: Call the sea-calves and swim out with them

effects.log: You swim out with the whole herd around you, and the sea-calves push the boat with their noses, steady as oxen, back to the beach. Afterwards you shake for an hour. The island never forgets.

choices.text: Run for the temple bell

effects.log: You run up and ring the temple bell until your arms ache. The grown-ups row back in time. The boat is caught at the very edge of the reef.

choices.text: Shout to the children to lie down in the boat

effects.log: You shout from the rocks until they hear: lie down, hold on. They do. The boat spins over the reef on a wave and lands, upright, in the lagoon. Everyone says it was luck. It was also you.

events.text: The islands of {pw_world} float in the sky, and the first thing every child learns is the Edge Rope: a long braided rope tied around every child's waist when they go out to play, fixed to a ring by the temple door. Your rope is blue, with a bell on the end, so the grown-ups can hear where you are.

choices.text: Run to the end of your rope

effects.log: You run until the rope pulls you up short, and stand at the very end of it, and look out at the clouds going by below your toes. Your bell rings and rings. You are not frightened at all.

choices.text: Tie your rope to a friend's

effects.log: You tie your rope to the next child's so you can go further together. The grown-ups are cross, then impressed. Now all the small children do it.

choices.text: Play close to the temple

effects.log: You play close to the temple door all summer, where the cloud-flowers grow. You know every one of them by the end of the year.

events.text: The Rope Day festival: the day the children of the islands are judged old enough for a longer rope. The priests measure each child against the god's own measure, a notched staff that is said to be the god's height, exactly.

choices.text: Stand tall against the god's staff

effects.log: You stand very straight against the staff. You come up to the third notch. The priest says that is where the god's heart would be, and gives you a rope twice as long.

choices.text: Ask why the god needed a measure

effects.log: The priest says that before the god made the islands the god measured them, to be sure they would hold a child. You think that is the kindest thing you have ever heard.

choices.text: Ask to keep your short rope

effects.log: You ask to keep your old rope one more year, because you like the bell. The priests allow it, and add a second bell.

events.text: A gust takes a little one from the next island right off the grass at the edge: the child is dangling now below the edge on the end of a short rope, bell ringing wildly, over the clouds. You are the closest.

choices.text: Haul the rope in, hand over hand

ok.log: You brace your feet and haul, hand over hand, until a small furious face comes up over the edge. You both sit in the grass and cry. The whole island comes running.

fail.log: You cannot lift the rope alone, but you hold it, burning your hands, until the grown-ups come and pull the child up. Your palms are bandaged for a month and every child on the island wants to see.

choices.text: Tie the child's rope to the temple ring and run for help

effects.log: You tie the rope off at the nearest ring with the knot the priests taught you, and run. The knot holds. The priests say your knot will be taught to every child.

choices.text: Climb down to the child on your own long rope

effects.log: You go over the edge on your long rope and hold the little one until help comes, both of you swinging over the clouds, singing the rope song to keep from being afraid.

events.text: On the great continent of {pw_world} the harvest ends with the Harvest Run: every child of the farms runs from the last field to the temple, carrying one ear of grain for the god, and the first child to lay it on the altar is called Swift for a year.

choices.text: Run as fast as you can

effects.log: You run so fast you drop your grain halfway and have to go back for it. You come in eleventh, holding a very battered ear of wheat. The priest says the god likes them battered.

choices.text: Run with the slowest child

effects.log: You run with the smallest child, who has short legs and a big heart. You come in last together, to the loudest cheer of the day.

choices.text: Take the shortcut through the orchard

effects.log: You take the shortcut through the orchard and are caught by a goose, and arrive late, honking. It becomes a story the whole farm tells.

events.text: This year you have trained. All summer, up and down the field paths with a stick for an ear of grain. On the morning of the Harvest Run your legs feel like springs.

choices.text: Run for Swift

ok.log: You lay your ear of grain on the altar first, gasping, and the priest calls you Swift. For a year people nod to you on the road. A grandmother gives you a pie for no reason.

fail.log: You come in second, a whisker behind a farmer's child from the next valley. You both lie on the temple steps laughing. You have a rival, and a friend.

choices.text: Run to the god's old way stone instead

effects.log: You run not to the temple but to the old way-stone on the hill, where the god is said to have stood and looked at the whole continent. You lay your grain there, alone, and the wind takes it.

choices.text: Help carry the old priest's chair to the finish

effects.log: The old priest can no longer walk to the finish, so you and two others carry the chair. You see the whole race from beside the priest, who tells you who will win, every time.

events.text: The Harvest Run has a new rule this year, decided by the elders: the winner must give a speech at the temple, thanking the god for the harvest. The children are horrified. Nobody wants to win.

choices.text: Win, and make the speech

effects.log: You win, and stand on the temple steps and say: thank you for the wheat, and for the legs. The crowd laughs and then claps for a long time.

choices.text: Arrange a tie with every runner

effects.log: You arrange it so all the children cross the line holding hands. The elders cannot decide who must speak. So, terrified, the children speak together.

choices.text: Run slowly and enjoy the view

effects.log: You run slowly and look at the gold fields under the sky, and think that whoever made all this did it well. You come in somewhere in the middle and are perfectly happy.

events.text: In the high valleys of {pw_world} the children herd the goats, and every child gets a goat bell of their own, cast at the temple with a different note. The priests say the god listens to the mountains by their bells.

choices.text: Choose the deepest bell

effects.log: Your bell sounds like a bigger animal than any goat. The goats respect it. So do the other children.

choices.text: Choose the highest bell

effects.log: Your bell is a thin bright ting, like a star if a star made a sound. You can hear it across three valleys.

choices.text: Ask the priest which bell the god likes best

effects.log: The priest laughs and says the god likes the cracked ones best, because they sound like people. You choose the cracked one.

events.text: A cloud has come down on the high pasture, thick as wool, and your goats are scattered in it. You cannot see your own hand. Somewhere a cliff is waiting for a careless goat, or a careless child.

choices.text: Ring your bell and wait for them to come

effects.log: You stand still and ring your bell. One by one the goats come out of the cloud to its note, and you count them all home. Not one lost.

choices.text: Sit down until the cloud lifts

effects.log: You sit down where you are, as the old herders taught. The cloud lifts by noon. All the goats are grazing quietly ten steps away, laughing at you.

choices.text: Go after the lead goat

ok.log: You find the lead goat by its smell and follow it home, and the others follow it. You arrive soaked, proud and covered in burrs.

fail.log: You slip on the wet grass and slide a good way down the slope on your back. Nothing is broken but your pride and your trousers. The goats come home on their own.

events.text: The Bell Festival, when every goat bell of the valley is rung at once at sunset, a great clanging prayer up the mountainside, so that the god will know the valley is still here.

choices.text: Ring your bell from the highest rock

effects.log: You climb the highest rock and ring your bell into the red sky. Below you the whole valley rings back. It is the loudest, happiest noise you have ever been part of.

choices.text: Stay silent, and listen to the valley

effects.log: You hold your bell still and listen. Every bell is different. You can hear every family in the valley. It sounds, you think, like a world talking to its maker.

choices.text: Lend your bell to a child who has none

effects.log: A child new to the valley has no bell yet. You give yours. The child rings it so hard the clapper flies off. Everyone laughs and the priest casts a new one for free.

events.text: The River Folk children of {pw_world} make reed boats as soon as they can tie a knot, and race them down to the god's ford, where the first of the River Folk crossed, the priests say, holding the god's hand.

choices.text: Make a big, slow boat

effects.log: Your boat is wide and steady and carries a frog all the way to the ford. The frog seems pleased. So are you.

choices.text: Make a small, fast boat

effects.log: Your boat is thin as a leaf and wins by a length. You are unbearable for a week.

choices.text: Help the little ones tie their knots

effects.log: You spend the morning tying knots for the little ones. Every boat in the race is held together by your hands. That feels better than winning.

events.text: The reed harvest: the River Folk children cut reeds along the bank for thatch, mats and baskets, singing the cutting song, which is about the god teaching the first River Folk how to weave. The work is wet and hard and full of eels.

choices.text: Sing loudest

effects.log: You sing the cutting song so loudly the grown-ups join in across the river. The reeds are cut by noon. Everyone says you have a River Folk voice.

choices.text: Weave something new

effects.log: You weave the cut reeds into a little figure of the god, standing in water. The priests put it in the temple. It is still there, browning, years later.

choices.text: Catch an eel with your bare hands

effects.log: You catch an eel with your bare hands and it gets away with great dignity. Then you catch another. You eat well that night.

events.text: The river has risen in the night, and the god's ford is under brown water. The old ferryman says only someone small and quick can take a rope across on a reed raft, so the ford-line can be strung for the families on the far bank.

choices.text: Pole the reed raft across

ok.log: You pole the reed raft across the brown water with the rope tied round you, and tie it to the old post on the far side. The families come across on the line all afternoon.

fail.log: The current spins you round twice and you land downstream in a willow, soaked and furious. But the rope reaches, and the grown-ups do the rest.

choices.text: Send your fast little boat across with a thin line

effects.log: You tie a fishing line to your fastest boat and set it on the current at just the right angle. It lands on the far bank. The rope follows the line. The ferryman stares at you.

choices.text: Run to the bridge upriver and tell the far bank

effects.log: You run three miles to the old bridge and down the other side and tell the far bank to wait. You arrive with bleeding feet and the families wait, and are safe.

events.text: Stone-Born children do not fight; they push. The game is played on a circle of sand with a round stone the size of a melon, and two children push it from opposite sides until one of them gives ground. The priests say the god taught the first Stone-Born this game, so that they would grow strong without breaking each other.

choices.text: Push with all your strength

effects.log: You push until your face is red and your feet dig trenches. You lose, but the other child is so tired afterwards that you both lie down in the sand and laugh.

choices.text: Push slowly and wait for the other child to tire

effects.log: You push gently and steadily, and the other child pushes too hard, and tires, and you win. The old people nod: that is the Stone-Born way.

choices.text: Watch the champions instead

effects.log: You watch the oldest children push, and notice that the best of them breathe out as they push. You try it at home against the door.

events.text: Your turn to push the temple stone: the great one, older than the town, that every Stone-Born child must try to move an inch on the feast of the god. Nobody under twelve has ever moved it.

choices.text: Push the temple stone

ok.log: You push until the world goes white at the edges, and the stone moves the width of a fingernail. The priests measure it twice. The town talks of nothing else for a month.

fail.log: The stone does not move. Nobody expected it to. The priest clasps your shoulder and says the stone has felt your hands and will remember them.

choices.text: Lean on it and wait

effects.log: You lean your back on the stone and push with your legs, slowly, without stopping. It does not move. But the priests say you pushed longest of any child they have seen.

choices.text: Ask the stone politely

effects.log: You put your hands on the stone and ask it, politely, to move for you. It does not. The grown-ups laugh, but kindly, and an old warrior says she asked the same thing at your age.

events.text: A new family has come to your town from the low lands, and their child does not know the pushing game, and has been pushed out of every circle. The child is sitting alone on the wall.

choices.text: Teach the child the game, slowly

effects.log: You teach the newcomer to push from the hips and breathe out. In a month the child wins a match, and everybody cheers, because that is also the Stone-Born way.

choices.text: Invite the child to push with you, together, against the temple stone

effects.log: You push together against the great stone. It does not move. But afterwards the newcomer sits with you at lunch, and is never alone again.

choices.text: Ask the child to teach you a game from the low lands

effects.log: The child teaches you a low-land game with knucklebones. Soon half the town is playing it. The old warriors are scandalised and secretly very good at it.

events.text: The Wind Kin children of {pw_world} learn their letters from wind-chimes: every letter has a chime of its own hung in the temple porch, and when the wind blows, the porch spells words. The priests say the god's first words to the Wind Kin were spoken on the wind, and they have been listening ever since.

choices.text: Learn every chime by ear

effects.log: You learn every chime by ear in a month, and walk home spelling the wind out loud. A cross neighbour says the wind is saying turnip. You say the wind is saying it badly.

choices.text: Make your own chime from a spoon

effects.log: You make a chime from a stolen spoon and hang it in the porch. It is a letter nobody knows. The priests argue about it all autumn.

choices.text: Lie under the porch and listen

effects.log: You lie on the porch boards and listen until the chimes stop being letters and become something else, like breathing. You fall asleep and dream in words.

events.text: A storm-night, and the temple porch is ringing like mad: chimes crashing into each other, spelling out nonsense, the whole valley awake. The old people say on storm-nights the wind sometimes spells true things.

choices.text: Write down every letter it rings

effects.log: You sit up all night with a candle and write down every chime. In the morning you have pages of nonsense, and one clear word in the middle of it: here. You keep the page.

choices.text: Go out and hold the chimes still

effects.log: You go out into the wind and hold the chimes still, one by one, so the valley can sleep. You come back soaked. The priests are cross and grateful.

choices.text: Sing back at the wind

effects.log: You stand in the door and sing a nonsense song back at the chimes. The wind seems to falter. The grown-ups pull you in, laughing.

events.text: The Wind Kin children send a message to the god every year on the high hill: each one rings a chime with one letter, and together they spell a word for the wind to carry. This year the children must choose the word, and they are arguing.

choices.text: Suggest the word thanks

effects.log: Thanks it is. The children ring it out across the hill, letter by letter, and the wind takes it away east, where the priests say the god lives.

choices.text: Suggest the word come

effects.log: The children ring out come. The old people watching from the bottom of the hill go very quiet. Nobody has sent that word in a hundred years.

choices.text: Suggest the word why

effects.log: Why, ring the chimes, one letter at a time. The priests are horrified, then thoughtful. The wind carries it a very long way.

events.text: Every year on the day of the Blessing, when the priests say the god first {pw_record}, every household in {pw_world} bakes a round loaf and the children press their thumbs into the top, one thumbprint for each blessing.

choices.text: Press your thumb in carefully

effects.log: Your thumbprint is perfect, and the loaf rises around it like a little crater. The grown-ups say you have a baker's thumb.

choices.text: Press your whole hand in

effects.log: You press your whole hand in. The loaf rises into a strange flat star. It is the most talked-about loaf in the street.

choices.text: Eat the dough

effects.log: You eat so much of the dough that the loaf is small. Your stomach aches. The grown-ups say the god would understand. The god, you think, would have eaten it too.

events.text: The children are told the story of the first Blessing at the temple: how the fields failed, and the people prayed, and the god heard them. The priest asks the children what they would ask the god for, if the god came again.

choices.text: Ask for nothing, because the god already gave enough

effects.log: The priest looks at you for a long moment and then tells the whole class that this is the best answer anyone has given in twenty years.

choices.text: Ask for a blessing for someone poor

effects.log: You ask for a blessing for the old widower at the end of the lane, whose roof leaks. The priest does not wait for the god: the temple mends the roof that week.

choices.text: Ask why the god stopped

effects.log: The priest says the god never stopped; the god only does not need to do it twice. You are not sure that is true. Neither, you think, is the priest.

events.text: This year your loaf will go to the temple altar, chosen out of all the loaves in the street, and the whole street will watch it carried up. You have one chance to bake it.

choices.text: Bake it yourself

ok.log: Your loaf comes out of the oven golden, round and high, with every thumbprint sharp. The priest holds it up to the crowd. It is the best day of your year.

fail.log: Your loaf comes out flat and black on one side. The street carries it up anyway, singing. The priests say the god prefers honest bread.

choices.text: Bake it with the old widower

effects.log: You bake it with the old widower from the end of the lane, who was a baker once. The widower cries a little into the flour and makes the best loaf in years.

choices.text: Give your place to a child who never gets chosen

effects.log: You give your place to a shy child from the next street. The child bakes a crooked loaf and carries it up the steps, shining, and you are prouder than if it were yours.

events.text: The children of {pw_world} learn the Sorry Prayers before they learn to count: short apologies to the sky, said every morning, because the priests teach that the god {pw_record}, and that a world must always be a little sorry, just in case.

choices.text: Say them every morning

effects.log: You say them every morning, very carefully, sorry for the weeds and sorry for the noise and sorry for the stolen apple. You feel much better and slightly suspicious.

choices.text: Ask what the world did wrong

effects.log: The priest says nobody quite remembers what the world did wrong, only that the god was angry. You decide to find out.

choices.text: Make up a thank-you prayer instead

effects.log: You make up a thank-you prayer and say it very quietly after the sorry ones. Nobody notices. You keep saying it.

events.text: A thunderstorm, the worst for years. The children are herded into the temple to say the Sorry Prayers until it stops. The thunder shakes the shutters. The smallest children are crying.

choices.text: Tell the little ones the god is not angry with them

effects.log: You tell them the god cannot be angry with anyone so small, and that the thunder is only the sky moving its furniture. They stop crying. A priest overhears and says nothing.

choices.text: Say your thank-you prayer out loud

effects.log: In a gap in the thunder you say your thank-you prayer out loud: thank you for the roof, the bread and the cat. The children copy it. The storm passes soon after.

choices.text: Count the seconds between flash and thunder

effects.log: You count the seconds aloud, the way a fisherman showed you, and tell everyone the storm is going away. It is. The priests are startled to find a child who knows.

events.text: You have found it, in the oldest scrolls at the back of the temple library: the record of why the god punished the world. It is a short, plain entry: the year, the punishment, and nothing else. No reason written.

choices.text: Tell the priest what you found

effects.log: The priest reads it twice and sits down heavily. 'No reason,' the priest says. 'All these years of sorry.' The next morning, for the first time, the temple adds a thank-you to the Sorry Prayers.

choices.text: Write a reason in the margin yourself

effects.log: You write, small, in the margin: because it was tired, and is sorry too. You have no idea why you wrote that. You feel, somehow, that it is true.

choices.text: Put the scroll back and keep saying the prayers

effects.log: You put the scroll back. The prayers are a comfort to people, whatever the reason. You say them every morning, and add your thank-you.

events.text: In {pw_world} every house keeps an empty chair at the table for the god, who made the world and then was silent, and has never once come to supper. The chair is dusted every day. Children are not allowed to sit in it.

choices.text: Sit in it when nobody is looking

effects.log: You sit in the god's chair when nobody is looking. It is exactly your size. You climb down quickly, with a strange warm feeling, as if you had been somewhere you belong.

choices.text: Put your bread on it, for the god

effects.log: You put half your bread on the empty chair. In the morning it is gone. It was probably the dog. Probably.

choices.text: Ask why the god never comes

effects.log: The old people say the god is shy, and very busy, and might come any day, so the chair must be ready. You check the chair every evening for a year.

events.text: A traveller comes to supper, a stranger, tired and wet, and there is no seat for them, only the god's chair. The grown-ups look at each other. Nobody has ever sat in the god's chair at supper.

choices.text: Tell the traveller to sit in the god's chair

effects.log: You say the god would want the traveller to sit. The grown-ups look shocked, then relieved. The traveller sits, and eats, and tells the best stories you have ever heard.

choices.text: Give the traveller your own seat

effects.log: You give up your stool and eat standing at the window. The traveller notices, and before leaving, gives you a carved bird, and says you will make a good host.

choices.text: Say you will sit in the god's chair yourself, so the traveller can have yours

effects.log: You sit in the god's chair. It is still exactly your size. The traveller looks at you for a long moment, and smiles, and says nothing.

events.text: The temple school asks the children to write down what they would say to the god, if the god ever came to sit in the empty chair. The best letter will be read at the feast.

choices.text: Write: you can come any time

effects.log: You write: you can come any time, we have kept your chair, and the soup is good. Your letter is read at the feast. Grown-ups are seen wiping their eyes.

choices.text: Write: why were you silent?

effects.log: You write it plainly: why were you silent? The priest reads it at the feast. Nobody has asked that aloud before. The silence afterwards is very long, and not unkind.

choices.text: Leave the page blank

effects.log: You hand in a blank page. The teacher is angry until you explain: that is what the god said to us. The teacher keeps your page.

events.text: Because the god once walked among the people of {pw_world} in disguise, the children play the Stranger Game: every stranger who comes to town might be the god, and the first child to spot the god wins. Nobody has ever won. The strangers are mostly tinkers.

choices.text: Follow a tinker all day

effects.log: You follow a tinker all day, taking notes. The tinker is not the god. The tinker is, however, very good at mending pots, and teaches you how.

choices.text: Ask every stranger straight out

effects.log: You ask a tinker, a goose-girl and a merchant whether they are the god. The merchant says yes, for a coin. You decide the merchant is lying. The goose-girl does not answer, which is suspicious.

choices.text: Decide the god is a dog

effects.log: You decide the god would come as a dog, and you feed every stray in town. You do not win the game, but you are the most popular child with dogs in the history of {pw_world}.

events.text: The priests tell the children what the god was like when the god walked among them: ordinary, they say. Ordinary clothes, ordinary face, a little tired, kind to children, bad at haggling. The children are disappointed.

choices.text: Say that sounds like anyone

effects.log: You say that sounds like anyone. The priest says: yes, that is rather the point. You walk home looking at everyone differently.

choices.text: Say that sounds like you

effects.log: You say it sounds like you. Everybody laughs. The oldest priest does not laugh, and looks at you for a long time over the top of the scroll.

choices.text: Ask the goose-girl again

effects.log: You go and ask the goose-girl again. She says, quite seriously, that she is not the god, but that she has thought about it, and would like to be asked again later.

events.text: A very ordinary stranger comes to town, tired, kind to children, terrible at haggling. Every child in the Stranger Game is following them in a line. The stranger is starting to look nervous.

choices.text: Tell the other children to leave the stranger alone

effects.log: You call off the game and apologise. The stranger is so relieved that they buy every child a pear. It is a very good pear. You will never know.

choices.text: Ask the stranger to haggle for you at the market

effects.log: The stranger haggles for your apples and loses badly, and pays the difference out of their own pocket, laughing. You have never been more certain of anything.

choices.text: Look in the mirror instead

effects.log: You go home and look into the water bucket, and think that if the god walked among people as an ordinary person, then anyone could be the god, even you. You go to bed very thoughtful.

events.text: In {pw_world} children are taught to fear the god: the god {pw_record}, and the skipping rhymes are about hiding from the sky. Duck your head, the god is watching, close the shutters, keep it secret. You skip to it every day without thinking.

choices.text: Skip the rhyme with everyone

effects.log: You skip the rhyme until you can do it backwards. The grown-ups nod approvingly. You duck your head every time a cloud passes, for years.

choices.text: Change the words when nobody is listening

effects.log: You change the words: lift your head, the god is watching, open the shutters, wave hello. You sing it only to yourself, under the blanket.

choices.text: Ask your friends what the god is like

effects.log: Your friends say the god is enormous, angry and has teeth. You think a god with teeth would not make lamp-flowers and kittens, and say so.

events.text: A temple school lesson on the god's punishments, with frightening pictures. A small child at the back is crying. The teacher says fear is good for children: it keeps them from doing wrong.

choices.text: Say the god might have been sorry

effects.log: You say, quite loudly, that the god might have been sorry afterwards. The class goes silent. You are sent out. Outside, an old gardener says, under his breath, that he always thought so too.

choices.text: Sit by the crying child

effects.log: You sit by the crying child and whisper your new rhyme. Lift your head, the god is watching, wave hello. The child stops crying, and giggles, and the teacher cannot tell why.

choices.text: Draw the god kind in the margin of your slate

effects.log: You draw the god with a kind face in the corner of your slate. The teacher wipes it off. You draw it again the next day. And the next.

events.text: Your new rhyme has spread. Children in three streets are skipping it: lift your head, wave hello. A priest has come to the square to find out who started it.

choices.text: Own up

effects.log: You step forward. The priest looks at you for a long time and then, unexpectedly, asks you to sing it. You do. The priest walks away without a word, and the next week the temple stops teaching the old rhyme.

choices.text: Say nobody knows who started it

effects.log: You say it just grew, like moss. It is almost true. The priest gives up and goes home, humming it.

choices.text: Ask the priest whether the god can hear children

effects.log: The priest says yes, every word. Then, you say, the god has heard us say hello. The priest has no answer to that.

events.text: In {pw_world} almost nobody remembers that the world was made at all. But your great-grandmother, who is very old and sits by the stove, still remembers the god's name from her own grandmother, and sometimes says it in her sleep.

choices.text: Ask her to tell you the god's name

effects.log: She whispers it in your ear, with her dry old hand on your cheek. It is a strange, warm word. It feels like a word you had forgotten yourself.

choices.text: Bring her tea and listen to her stories

effects.log: You bring her tea every afternoon, and she tells you stories nobody else remembers: of a world that was once new, and someone who made it, and went away.

choices.text: Play by the stove and only half listen

effects.log: You play with your wooden animals by the stove while she talks. You only half listen. Years later, you find you remember every word.

events.text: Your great-grandmother has asked you to help her to the old shrine on the hill, the one with no roof and no priest, where she says people once prayed to the god whose name she knows. Nobody else will take her.

choices.text: Take her, slowly, all morning

effects.log: It takes all morning. At the shrine she puts her hand on the stone and says the name, out loud, for the first time in fifty years. The wind changes. She smiles like a girl.

choices.text: Say the name with her

effects.log: You say the name together at the shrine, two voices, one very old and one very young. A bird lands on the stone and looks at you both, its head on one side.

choices.text: Bring the whole family

effects.log: You talk the whole family into coming. They complain all the way up. At the top they go quiet. Your father says he had forgotten there was a shrine at all.

events.text: Your great-grandmother has died, in her sleep, by the stove, very old and very peaceful. At the funeral nobody knows what prayer to say for her, because nobody remembers the old prayers. Everyone looks at the ground.

choices.text: Say the god's name over her

effects.log: You step forward and say the name she taught you. The family looks up. Your mother squeezes your hand. Afterwards three neighbours ask you, quietly, what the word was.

choices.text: Tell one of her stories

effects.log: You tell her story of the world when it was new. Your voice shakes and then steadies. When you finish, even the neighbours are crying, and nobody says it is only a story.

choices.text: Stand quietly with your family

effects.log: You stand with your family and hold your mother's hand. Some things do not need words, even old ones.

events.text: There are two altars in your town now: the old one of the god who made {pw_world}, chipped and quiet, and the new one of a shining god whose priests wear gold and hand out sugared almonds to children every morning.

choices.text: Take the almonds

effects.log: You take the sugared almonds. They are very good. The priests in gold smile at you a little too widely, and ask your name.

choices.text: Take the almonds and leave one at the old altar

effects.log: You take the almonds and leave one on the old chipped altar. It seems only fair. The next morning, there is a pebble in its place, smooth and warm.

choices.text: Go to the old altar instead

effects.log: You go to the old altar, where there is only an old priest sweeping. The old priest gives you a broom, and you sweep together, and it is strangely pleasant.

events.text: The priests in gold are telling the children that their shining god made the world. You know the old story: that the world's god {pw_record}. The two stories do not agree, and the children are arguing in the yard.

choices.text: Tell the old story to the other children

effects.log: You tell the old story well, all of it. Some of the children believe you, and some do not, and all of them listen.

choices.text: Ask the priests in gold what their god has done

effects.log: You ask the priests in gold what their god actually did. They talk for a long time about gold. They do not answer the question. The children notice.

choices.text: Show the warm pebble

effects.log: You show the warm pebble from the old altar. It is still warm, a week later, in the cold. The children go quiet and pass it around carefully.

events.text: The old priest of the chipped altar is too old to climb the steps any more, and the old altar is going to be taken away. The old priest asks the children, without much hope, whether any of them would keep it clean.

choices.text: Keep it clean, every week

effects.log: You sweep it every week, bring flowers in summer and candles in winter. Other children start coming. By the next spring the old altar has more visitors than in twenty years.

choices.text: Help the old priest up the steps instead

effects.log: You and two friends carry the old priest up the steps on a chair, every morning, so that the old altar stays open. It is hard work. The old priest weeps every time.

choices.text: Make a little altar at home

effects.log: You make a little altar to the old god in a corner at home: a stone, a candle, a flower. It is enough, you think. The old priest says so too.

events.text: In {pw_world} the law is that the dead may speak once to those who loved them, and every child grows up knowing it, the way children elsewhere know that fire is hot. The old dog of your house, Biscuit, is very old now, and grey in the face, and sleeps in the sun most of the day.

choices.text: Spend every afternoon with Biscuit

effects.log: You spend every afternoon lying in the sun with Biscuit, telling it everything. It thumps its tail at the good parts.

choices.text: Teach Biscuit one last trick

effects.log: You teach the old dog to shake paws. It takes a month. Biscuit does it once, perfectly, and then never again, as if to say: there.

choices.text: Ask the grown-ups if dogs can speak once too

effects.log: The grown-ups do not know. The priest does not know. Nobody has ever asked. You are given a sweet to stop asking.

events.text: Biscuit has died, in the sun, in the night. You are sad in a way you did not know about before. And that evening, at the door where the old dog used to wait, you hear something.

choices.text: Listen

effects.log: It is not words. It is the sound of a tail thumping on boards, and then a voice like warm bread saying, quite clearly: good. Then it is gone. You sit on the doorstep for a long time.

choices.text: Run and fetch the grown-ups

effects.log: You fetch the grown-ups, but by the time they come the doorstep is quiet. They hold you while you cry. They believe you, which helps more than anything.

choices.text: Say goodbye back

effects.log: You say goodbye to the empty doorstep, out loud. The evening air seems to settle, like a dog lying down. You feel better.

events.text: A younger child in your street has lost a grandfather, and has not heard anything, and is frightened that it means the grandfather did not love them. The child comes to you, because everyone knows about Biscuit.

choices.text: Tell the child the law says once, not soon

effects.log: You say that once might be any time, even years from now, at the right moment. The child stops crying. Three years later, the child knocks on your door to tell you it happened.

choices.text: Sit with the child at the grandfather's door

effects.log: You sit with the child on the grandfather's step every evening for a week. Nothing happens. But on the seventh evening the child says: I think he is just being quiet. That is enough.

choices.text: Take the child to the priest

effects.log: The priest tells the child kindly that the once-voice comes in its own time, and some people hear it as a feeling, not a voice. The child goes home thoughtful.

events.text: In {pw_world}, where what is sown is reaped, every child is given a clay jar at the temple and a handful of beans. A white bean goes in for a kindness, a black bean for an unkindness. At the end of the year the priests count the jars, and nobody wants a dark jar.

choices.text: Fill yours with white beans honestly

effects.log: You do kindnesses all year: carrying water, sharing bread, finding a lost goat. Your jar is nearly white. You are very pleased with yourself, which you suspect counts as a black bean.

choices.text: Put in black beans when you deserve them

effects.log: You put in every black bean you earn, honestly, even for the stolen plum. Your jar is speckled. The priest says it is the most honest jar of the year.

choices.text: Plant the beans instead

effects.log: You plant your beans in the garden to see what grows. Black and white come up the same green. You think about that for a long time.

events.text: A child in your class has a very dark jar this year, nearly all black, and the other children will not play with them. The child sits alone at the edge of the yard with the jar.

choices.text: Go and play with the child

effects.log: You go and play with the child, who is clumsy and quick-tempered and very funny. You put a white bean in your jar for it. Then you take it out again, because that is not why you did it.

choices.text: Give the child some of your white beans

effects.log: You pour half your white beans into the child's jar. The priests catch you. They are about to be angry, and then they look at each other, and one of them laughs.

choices.text: Ask why the child has so many black beans
