effects.log: The child says: because I put them all in. Nobody else does. You think about your own jar, and go home, and add three.

events.text: Counting Day at the temple. The priests line up the jars of every child in town. The old high priest walks the line slowly, and stops at yours.

choices.text: Say what you learned

effects.log: You say you learned that kindness does not need counting, but it helps to notice. The high priest nods slowly and says the law of the world is the same.

choices.text: Pour your jar out onto the temple floor

effects.log: You tip the jar out, black and white together, and say: they all grew the same. The high priest looks at the beans for a long time, and lets them lie.

choices.text: Smile and say nothing

effects.log: You say nothing. The high priest smiles back and moves on. Some things, you think, are between you and the world.

events.text: In {pw_world} storms come only where they are owed. So when a little storm-cloud comes over the hill on a fine morning and stops directly over your house, the whole street comes out to see who has done something.

choices.text: Confess to the stolen honey

effects.log: You confess to the stolen honey. The cloud drizzles on you, briefly and specifically, and goes away. The street applauds. The beekeeper makes you return a full jar.

choices.text: Say nothing and stay under the eaves

effects.log: You stay under the eaves. The cloud stays too. After an hour the street is bored and goes home, and the cloud rains on your washing, thoroughly.

choices.text: Point out that the cloud is over the neighbour's goat

effects.log: You point out, correctly, that the cloud has moved over the neighbour's goat, who has eaten three hats. The goat is drenched. Justice is done.

events.text: A storm the size of a small cloud keeps following one boy in your class, the miller's son, everywhere he goes, dripping on him. He says he has done nothing. Nobody believes him. He is very wet and very unhappy.

choices.text: Help him work out what he owes

effects.log: You sit with him under the dripping cloud and go through everything. At last he remembers: he promised his sister a kite and never made it. You make the kite together. The cloud goes.

choices.text: Stand under the cloud with him

effects.log: You stand under the cloud with him, getting wet out of friendship. The cloud seems confused, and thins out, and rains on both of you half as much.

choices.text: Ask the priest whether storms can be wrong

effects.log: The priest says the law is never wrong, but people are often wrong about what the law means. You are not sure that helps. It helps the miller's son a little.

events.text: A great storm is coming, the biggest anyone has seen, and it is heading for the whole town. Everyone is frightened, and everyone is confessing to everything, all at once, in the square. It is chaos.

choices.text: Ask what the whole town owes

effects.log: You stand on the well and ask: what does the whole town owe? There is a silence. Then someone mentions the old bridge the town promised the next village and never built. The town builds it. The storm passes over and rains on the river.

choices.text: Help the old and the small into the temple

effects.log: You spend the storm helping the old and the small into the temple. The storm turns out to be owed to the hills, which needed it. Nobody remembers who was confessing what.

choices.text: Watch where it goes

effects.log: You climb to the bell tower and watch. The storm goes round the town and empties itself on the dry hills behind it. You realise not every storm is a punishment.

events.text: In {pw_world} every river reaches the sea. It is the law of the world. So the children write notes on paper boats and set them on the stream behind the temple, and believe that every one of them will get there, however long it takes.

choices.text: Write a note to the sea

effects.log: You write, in large uneven letters: hello sea, from me. You set it on the water and watch it out of sight round the bend.

choices.text: Write a note to the god

effects.log: You write: dear god, the river is nice, thank you. You set it on the water. A priest who is watching from the bridge takes off his hat.

choices.text: Follow the boat as far as you can

effects.log: You follow your boat along the bank for three fields, until your legs give out. It goes on without you, bobbing. You feel very small and very hopeful.

events.text: A fisherman's child from the coast comes to your town, far downriver, with a story: on the beach where the river meets the sea there are paper boats, thousands of them, and the coast children read them all.

choices.text: Ask if anyone found yours

effects.log: The child does not know. But the child says the coast children write answers and send them back up the river with traders. You go and look at every trader's cart for a month.

choices.text: Send another boat, for the coast children

effects.log: You write a new boat: to whoever reads this, I hope your sea is nice. You set it on the stream, with the coast child watching. It seems a good thing to do.

choices.text: Ask the coast child what the sea is like

effects.log: The child talks for an hour about the sea: bigger than the sky, saltier than tears, louder than the temple bell. You go home and dream of it every night for a week.

events.text: A trader stops at your door with a small package, carried up from the coast, wrapped in oilcloth. Inside is your own paper boat, years old, water-stained and soft, and a note in a stranger's child's hand.

choices.text: Read the note

effects.log: It says: hello, from the sea. We got it. We have kept it with the others. It is a good boat. You read it twenty times. You keep the boat and the note in a box all your life.

choices.text: Write back, at once

effects.log: You write back that night, and set the letter on the stream at dawn. You know, because it is the law of the world, that it will get there.

choices.text: Show it to the priest by the bridge

effects.log: The old priest holds the stained boat and laughs, and says that every river reaches the sea, and sometimes the sea writes back. You both stand on the bridge a while.

events.text: The descendants of {pw_beast}, the first creature of {pw_world}, still live in the hills above your village, and every few years one of them brings a cub down to the temple meadow. This spring the cub has wandered off from its mother and is sitting in your garden, eating the cabbages.

choices.text: Share the cabbages

effects.log: You sit with the cub and feed it cabbages one by one until it falls asleep with its head on your foot. Its mother comes at dusk and looks at you for a long time, and takes the cub home.

choices.text: Fetch a priest

effects.log: The priest comes running, and kneels, and the cub licks the priest's bald head. The priest says it is the luckiest day of the year, and you have caused it.

choices.text: Hide behind the door and watch

effects.log: You watch the cub through the crack in the door. It knows you are there. Now and then it looks at the door, and you are sure it smiles.

events.text: The cub has come back to your garden, a year bigger, and seems to think you belong to it. The village children are jealous. The priests say a child chosen by the descendants of {pw_beast} is meant to learn something.

choices.text: Learn the cub's ways

effects.log: You follow the cub around the hills all summer and learn which roots are sweet, which streams are cold, and how to sleep in the sun without caring about anything.

choices.text: Bring the village children to play with it

effects.log: You bring the other children, one at a time, and introduce them. The cub knocks every one of them over gently. The jealousy goes out of the village like air from a bag.

choices.text: Ask the priests what you are meant to learn

effects.log: The priests argue about it for a week. In the end the oldest says you are meant to learn that the world was here before the people. You think the cub already taught you that.

events.text: The cub is nearly grown, enormous now, and the time has come for it to go up into the high hills with its own kind. It comes to your garden one last time, at dawn, and puts its great head against your chest.

choices.text: Walk with it to the foot of the hills

effects.log: You walk with it to the foot of the hills, your hand in its fur. At the first rock it stops, and you stop. It goes on. On clear nights, for years after, you hear it calling from the peaks.

choices.text: Give it something to remember you by

effects.log: You tie your hair-ribbon around its great foreleg. Years later, hunters in the hills tell of a huge beast with a faded ribbon who leads lost travellers home.

choices.text: Let it go without following

effects.log: You stand at the gate and let it go without following. It looks back once. You lift your hand. It is the hardest and best thing you have ever done.

events.text: {pw_world} is old, {pw_years} years old, and its hills are full of the ruins of kingdoms that rose and rested before your town was built. The children play in them: broken towers, mosaic floors, a stone throne in a field of poppies.

choices.text: Sit on the stone throne

effects.log: You sit on the old throne and rule the poppy field for an afternoon. Your subjects are bees. It is a peaceful reign.

choices.text: Clean a mosaic floor

effects.log: You brush the dirt off an old mosaic with your hands. Under it, in faded tiles, is a picture of the god holding up the sun. The face is gone. The hands are very clear.

choices.text: Collect broken tiles

effects.log: You collect a pocketful of coloured tiles, blue and gold and red. A neighbour sews them onto your coat so you glitter when you walk.

events.text: A scholar has come from the city to study the ruins, a thin, kind person with ink on every finger, and the children of the town have become the scholar's guides, for a copper a day.

choices.text: Show the scholar the mosaic of the god

effects.log: The scholar kneels at the mosaic for an hour without speaking. Then the scholar says it is the oldest picture of the god anyone has found, and writes your name in a notebook.

choices.text: Make up stories about every ruin

effects.log: You make up a story about every broken wall. The scholar writes them all down, and later puts them in a book, with a note: told by a child of the town, and probably not true.

choices.text: Ask the scholar how kingdoms end

effects.log: The scholar says kingdoms do not end, they rest, and the people go on. You look at the stone throne in the poppies and think that sounds right.

events.text: The scholar is leaving, and has asked the town's permission to take you along for a season, as an assistant: to see the great ruins of the old kingdoms and the libraries of the city. The town council says it is up to you.

choices.text: Go for the season

effects.log: You go. You see a library of ten thousand scrolls and a ruin as big as a mountain. You come home in autumn taller, quieter, and full of the long history of the world.

choices.text: Stay, and keep guiding the children

effects.log: You stay and take over the guiding of the younger children in the ruins. The scholar writes to you every year. The children call you the Keeper.

choices.text: Ask the scholar to send books instead

effects.log: You ask the scholar to send books. They come, a parcel every season, for years. You read every one in the poppy field, on the stone throne.
